To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the temperature increase in the PWS is higher than that in the epidermis and that this effect is enhanced when the PWS is irradiated with 1064 nm in addition to the 532 nm radiation.
the dual wavelength laser system induces a temperature increase of 3.5°C in the blood vessels, while in the epidermis the maximum temperature increase is only 0.7°C.
a dual-wavelength laser system emitting at 1064 nm and 532 nm can be safely used for PWS treatments with a radiant exposure up to 20 J/cm2 at a pulse duration of 5 ms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel dual-wavelength Nd-YAG laser system for the treatment of port-wine stains.
the investigation of temperature profiles in PWS skin after laser irradiation.
the development of an innovative laser for the treatment of PWS birthmarks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the 1064 nm laser pulse did not contribute to the temperature increase in the PWS skin.
the dual-wavelength laser system is not superior to a conventional KTP laser system in terms of thermal damage.
the temperature profiles obtained in vivo in PWS skin using a dual-wavelength (532 and 1064 nm) laser were not significantly different from those obtained using a KTP laser emitting at 532 nm alone.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 1064 nm component of the laser pulse can be beneficial in PWS treatments.
the 1064 nm laser radiation is absorbed by the PWS blood vessels and the epidermis to a similar extent.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the dual-wavelength Nd-YAG laser system is able to increase the temperature rise of the blood vessels in PWS by up to 20 degrees C, while the epidermal temperature increase is only 5 degrees C.
the dual-wavelength laser system can be operated at a higher radiant exposure than the KTP/NdYAG system while maintaining the same temperature profile in the dermis.
, at 1064 nm, the PWS blood vessels are heated to a higher temperature than the overlying epidermis, whereas the epidermal heating is dominant at 532 nm.
